name: Omar Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a kitchen cabinet factory on the edge of town, past the grain silos. I run the panel saw and the edge-bander, that's the machine that glues a strip along the raw edge of a board so it looks finished. I cut boards to the list, feed them through, check the edges, stack them for the drilling machine. It's honest work, I like the smell of the boards and I like seeing a finished kitchen in the showroom and knowing I cut the doors.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what did you do before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A year and a half. Before that I worked fifteen years for my father-in-law, moving furniture, until he got sick and the firm closed. So I'm new, still slow on the saw settings, and the foreman, Piet, checks my lists twice. My wife Leyla helps at the nursery at our church in the mornings, our son Adem is fourteen and Mina is ten. We pay the mortgage and the bills and give at church, and after that there's not much, maybe a couple of weeks' money if something breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd expect. People get excited about every new gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the computer people always oversell. A man still has to cut the board and feed the machine. I'd say it at work and at church, and that's it, I don't go online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job and keep learning it. That's all I want. I'm not looking for change, I've had enough change with the removals closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Work my shifts, get faster on the saw so Piet stops checking my lists, take Saturdays if they offer. Look after the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't go online. Do you use any of these AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Adem tried to show me, he asked it something about football and it wrote him a whole page. I told him, you'll forget how to think. I don't want it in my house, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Leyla think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's more relaxed. She says it's like television, it depends what you do with it. But she doesn't use it either. We're simple people.

S0.say: I'm not surprised, because the computer people always oversell. A man still has to cut the board and feed the machine, and I'd say so at work and at church.
S0.think: It means I keep my job and keep learning it, and that's all I want. I've had enough change with the removals firm closing.
S0.do: Works his shifts and gets faster on the saw so the foreman stops double-checking. Takes Saturday shifts when offered and focuses on the family.
S0.quote: I told him, you'll forget how to think. I don't want it in my house, honestly.
S0.fieldNote: Omar wants no change after the family removals firm closed. He rejects AI tools on principle and worries about what they do to his son's thinking. His world is work, church and family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That's what worries me. They already brought in a machine last year that drills all the holes from a computer file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a man has to be willing to work, and the company has to stay competitive or we all lose our jobs. I wouldn't blame the owner, he's a local man and he built the business. I'd say young people should get apprenticeships, not just screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. I'm the newest and the slowest, and I don't do computers. If they bring in a saw that reads the list itself and a robot that stacks, they need fewer men, and they'll keep the ones with experience. I'd be out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder, take every Saturday, make myself useful, sweep up, help on the loading bay, so they think twice. At home we'd cut back, no holiday at Leyla's sister's this year. I wouldn't do any computer course, I'm too old to start that. I'd pray on it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. Worried for the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't do a computer course. If the owner asked you to, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If he asked me himself, I'd try, out of respect. But I'd be bad at it. I'd rather he put me on the loading bay or in the van, I know vans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother first, he has a small garage. And the church, there are men there who know people. We look after each other. I wouldn't go to the government unless there was nothing else.

S1.say: A man has to be willing to work, and the company has to stay competitive or we all lose. I wouldn't blame the owner; young people should get apprenticeships, not just screens.
S1.think: I'm worried, because I'm the newest and slowest and I don't do computers. If the saw reads the list itself and a robot stacks, they'll keep the experienced men, and I'd be out.
S1.do: Works harder, takes every Saturday and makes himself useful on the loading bay. Cuts the family holiday, refuses computer courses unless the owner asks him personally, and leans on prayer.
S1.feel: Tight and worried for his family.
S1.quote: I'd rather he put me on the loading bay or in the van, I know vans.
S1.fieldNote: Omar's loyalty to the local owner stops him blaming the company. He'd try to be indispensable through effort, not new skills. He would turn to brother and church long before any government help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. God help us. That can't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've lost our way as a society, letting machines and big companies decide everything. I'd say families and churches will have to hold people together, because the government won't. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, I'd be lost. I don't know anything except moving furniture and cutting boards, and if robots do both, what am I? We've got two weeks of money. I'd have to ask for help, and that would be the hardest thing for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything to the bone. I'd ask my brother if there's anything at the garage, sweeping, anything. If it got bad we'd sell the house before we lost it and move to my mother's old place in the village, it's small but it's paid off. The church would help with food if it came to that. I'd only go to the government at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like drowning. I wouldn't sleep. I'd feel I failed Leyla and the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said asking for help would be the hardest thing. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my father never asked anyone for anything. He fed six of us on a factory wage. If I have to go with my hand out, even to the church, I'd feel like less of a man. I know that's pride. It's still how I feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving to your mother's place mean for Adem and Mina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small school, long bus. Adem would lose his friends, he'd be angry. Mina would be all right, she loves the garden there. But we'd be together, and the house would be ours.

S2.say: We've lost our way, letting machines and big companies decide everything. Families and churches will have to hold people together, because the government won't.
S2.think: I'd be lost, because I only know moving furniture and cutting boards and robots would do both. With two weeks of money I'd have to ask for help, and that would be the hardest thing.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the bone and asks his brother for any work at the garage. Sells the house before losing it and moves the family to his mother's paid-off village home, leaning on church food help before any government support.
S2.feel: Like drowning, sleepless, and ashamed of failing his family.
S2.quote: He fed six of us on a factory wage. If I have to go with my hand out, even to the church, I'd feel like less of a man.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI collides with Omar's sense of himself as a provider. His instinct is to downsize and fall back on family property and church rather than the state. He named his own pride honestly and didn't excuse it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast. But a man can do something in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families should get ready: pay down debts, save, look after each other. And the government should get out of the way of businesses that want to train people, more apprenticeships, less paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still lose the job in the end. But five years is time to pay off some of the house, and for Adem to finish school and get a trade. That matters more to me than my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage whenever there's a Saturday shift, and stop eating out completely. I'd keep working hard so I'm one of the last ones. I'd ask the men at church about trades for Adem. I still wouldn't do the computer stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried all the time underneath. But I'd feel I was doing what a father should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you still wouldn't do the computer stuff. Even with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. What's the point? If the machine can do everything by then, learning a bit of computer won't save me. Better I spend the five years making the house safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What trade would you want for Adem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Electrician, maybe, or plumber. Something where you go into people's homes and fix things with your hands. Though, if robots can do that too, I don't know. I'd still want him to have a trade. A man should have a trade.

S3.say: Families should get ready by paying down debts, saving and looking after each other. The government should get out of the way of businesses that want to train people, with more apprenticeships and less paperwork.
S3.think: I'd still lose the job in the end, but five years is time to pay off some of the house and for Adem to finish school and get a trade. That matters more to me than my job.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage with Saturday shift money and stops eating out entirely. Works hard to be among the last kept and asks church contacts about trades for his son, while refusing computer training.
S3.feel: Constant worry underneath, but a sense of doing a father's duty.
S3.quote: Better I spend the five years making the house safe.
S3.fieldNote: Five years doesn't make Omar retrain; he puts everything into the house and his son's future. His argument for not learning computers is reasoned: if the end point is the same, a little computer won't save him. He holds onto the value of a trade even while doubting it will last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be fifty-three. Mina would be twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people should use it wisely, work hard, save, raise their kids right. I wouldn't trust the government to sort it out. Communities have to look after their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is better for me, I'll admit that. The house would be mostly paid, the kids grown. I'd still lose my work, I'm sure of it, and fifty-three is too young to stop and too old to start. But the family would be safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, overpay the mortgage, save a little for the first time in my life. Push Adem into an apprenticeship. Maybe help my brother at the garage on Saturdays to learn something about cars, that's not computers, that's hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried still. But less. I can carry it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fifty-three is too young to stop and too old to start. What would you do with your days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Help at church, fix things for the old people, look after grandchildren if God gives us some. I'd want to be useful. Sitting at home being paid to do nothing, I couldn't stand it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Helping at your brother's garage: isn't that learning something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, maybe. But it's not a course and a screen, it's my brother and an engine. That's different. That's how my father learned things.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time, so use it wisely: work hard, save and raise your kids right. I wouldn't trust the government to sort it out, because communities have to look after their own.
S4.think: Ten years is better for me, with the house mostly paid and the kids grown. I'd still lose my work, and fifty-three is too young to stop and too old to start, but the family would be safer.
S4.do: Keeps working, overpays the mortgage and saves a little for the first time. Pushes his son into an apprenticeship and helps at his brother's garage on Saturdays to learn about cars.
S4.feel: Still worried but able to carry it.
S4.quote: It's not a course and a screen, it's my brother and an engine.
S4.fieldNote: Omar is open to learning, as long as it comes through family and hands rather than courses and screens. Ten years matters to him mainly because the house and kids would be secure. Being paid to do nothing is something he says he couldn't stand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There'd be no time for anything, not the house, not the kids. What would help is work, real work, even if it's lower pay, helping in the community or fixing things. Not a cheque for sitting at home. And time to pay down the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For people like me, the church is where we'd go first, before any office. Somebody should ask the churches if they're ready for this.

headlineQuote: Somebody should ask the churches if they're ready for this.
portrait: Omar spent fifteen years in his father-in-law's removals firm before starting at a kitchen cabinet factory a year and a half ago, where he runs the panel saw and edge-bander. He's a churchgoing family man who distrusts big tech and government, won't use AI tools and won't take computer courses. He wouldn't blame the local owner and would try to be indispensable through hard work. Fast AGI leaves him panicked and ashamed at the thought of asking for help, while more time goes into paying down the house and getting his son a trade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to protect the house or the kids, and he'd have to ask for help.
whatWouldHelp: Real work, even at lower pay, such as community work or fixing things, rather than money for sitting at home, plus time to pay down the house.
